name: Satin Pothos
description: Despite its common name, Satin Pothos is not a true pothos at all but a member of the Scindapsus genus - though it is grown and loved just like one. Its thick, heart-shaped leaves have a soft, matte, almost velvety texture and are dusted with shimmering silvery-grey spots and margins over deep green, giving the whole plant a satin sheen that catches the light beautifully. A naturally trailing and climbing vine, it looks stunning cascading from a shelf or hanging basket, and its variegation is naturally stable (silver markings, not chlorophyll-free white patches), so it holds its look reliably. Easy-going and forgiving, it tolerates a range of conditions but shows its best silvery contrast in medium-to-bright indirect light. Slightly slower-growing and more drought-tolerant than Golden Pothos, it is an excellent, elegant choice for beginners who want a trailing plant with more texture and shimmer.
toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and horses. Chewing it causes mouth pain and swelling, drooling, vomiting and difficulty swallowing.

symptoms: Pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and lips

careInstructions: Keep the soil moist but well drained during the growing season, and water less in winter - yellow leaves mean too much water, curling leaves too little
Provide medium to bright indirect light for the strongest silver variegation
Avoid harsh direct sun, which fades and scorches the leaves
Let it trail from a hanging basket or climb a small trellis or moss pole
Prune to encourage fuller, bushier growth
Propagates easily in water or soil from stem cuttings below a node
Wipe leaves gently to preserve the matte, silvery finish
Fertilize monthly during the growing season, and cut back in winter
commonProblems: Faded or dull silver markings: Too little light - move to a brighter spot
Yellow leaves: Overwatering - allow more drying between waterings
Brown, crispy leaf edges: Underwatering, low humidity, or sun scorch
Curling leaves: Underwatering or low humidity
Leggy growth with widely spaced leaves: Insufficient light
Root rot: Overwatering or poor drainage

fertilizing.tip: Fertilize monthly during the growing season, and cut back in winter

whatsNormal: Yellow leaves usually mean too much water; curling leaves mean too little.
Indoors it keeps its oval juvenile leaves; lobed adult leaves appear on mature climbing plants.

propagation.tip: Root 4-inch stem cuttings in spring or early summer.
